newsitem.title: ITALY: Overshadowed by Paris, Rome high fashion holds on.
newsitem.headline: Overshadowed by Paris, Rome high fashion holds on.

text.p: Life-size puppets depicting Italy's "first ladies" seated in the front row of design house Gattinoni's fashion show were a not-so-subtle appeal for attention.
Gattinoni's "provocation" in Rome high-fashion week posed the question: if women from Italy's political class don't come to the city's "alta moda" shows, who will?

"I wanted to have the pleasure, at least once, of having these women, who unlike those in Paris and New York, never frequent the 'alta moda' shows," Gattinoni president Stefano Dominella said, voicing a key lament at the Rome shows which end on Wednesday.
The puppets depicted Flavia Prodi, wife of prime minister Romano, Marianna Scalfaro, daughter of president Oscar Luigi, and Donatella Dini, wife of foreign minister Lamberto.
Gattinoni's complaint is part of a problem Rome designers have faced for years: the inability to regain their glory years of the 1960s and the dominance of Paris "haute couture".
Rome suffered its biggest blow in 1989 when Valentino, its best-known name, defected to Paris and never came back.
"You can't compare Paris and Rome," Dominella said in an interview. "France takes the prize for high fashion while Italy wins for its ready-to-wear designs shown in Milan."

Nevertheless, Rome's "alta moda", which presented its spring-summer fashions during four days of shows, has its niche and is holding on, Dominella said. "There is an international clientele who will always have money."
While Paris "haute couture" is famed for imaginative, cutting-edge designs, Rome is known for a traditional approach which never loses sight of its customers.
Those customers -- immaculately made-up and coiffured matrons -- turned out this week at a tent set up in the Villa Borghese park, where they sat in fur coats despite the balmy weather.
Fashion houses like the Furstenberg Collection gave them what they wanted: elegance for day and glamour for evening.
Furstenberg showed jackets with rounded necklines, nipped at the waist, flared over the hip and adorned with crystal buttons. They were worn over sleeveless shift dresses.
Evening gowns had beaded strapless bodices and satin skirts that bubbled slightly over the hips and fell to the ankle.

Andre Laug showed pastel-coloured pantsuits worn with simple white tank tops. Other suits had pleated skirts which never inched above the knee, worn with blouses with a big bow under the chin and tailored jackets.

Renato Balestra kept to basics with a collection dominated by floral and flowing design. He upheld "alta moda" tradition of painstaking attention to detail with a wedding gown to which he had attached layers of fabric orchid petals -- 2,000 in all.
Less traditional "enfant terrible" Gai Mattiolo, 29, staged an extravaganza with 99 Hong Kong-inspired designs.

Models wore silk suits in pearly white, pink and blue lined with gold-coloured embroidery and sequins. Kimono-like evening gowns had Chinese lettering or floral patterns in lacquered blues and reds. A contortionist from the Shanghai circus performed and singer Diana Ross also appeared on the catwalk.

Gattinoni's young designer Guillermo Mariotto also tried to break the mould. One model wore heavy black eye make-up and a spiky headpiece like a Mohawk Indian. She wore a tartan bustier, dog collar around her neck and a full-skirted ball gown.
The shows close on Wednesday evening with a Walt Disney-sponsored gala at which designers will dress the character Cruella De Vil from the film "101 Dalmatians".
